'''Paul Malone Allen''' (born September 1951) is an American cellular [[immunologist]] and current Robert L. Kroc Professor of Pathology and Immunology at [[Washington University School of Medicine]] in [[St. Louis]]. Allen holds prestigious MERIT status with the [[National Institutes of Health]].

==Education and career==
Paul Allen received his [[Bachelor of Science|bachelor's]] degree in 1974 from the [[University of Michigan]] followed by a [[Master of Science|master's]] degree in 1977 and a [[PhD|doctoral degree]] in 1981 with [[John Niederhuber]] and a thesis titled "Functional and serological examination of the central portion of the I region of the H-2 gene complex", both from the University of Michigan.<ref name=AAI>{{cite journal|doi=10.4049/jimmunol.177.3.1369 |pmid=16849437 |title=Defining Yourself: Tolerance Development in the Immune System |journal=The Journal of Immunology |volume=177 |issue=3 |pages=1369–1372 |year=2006 |last1=Allen |first1=Paul M. |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=fac>{{cite web|url=https://pathology.wustl.edu/people/paul-allen-phd/ |accessdate=15 July 2019 |title=Paul Allen, PhD |publisher=Washington University School of Medicine}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|title=ProQuest Dissertations and Theses – Paul Malone Allen |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/303128284 |accessdate=15 July 2019|year=1981 |id={{ProQuest|303128284}} |type=Ph.D  }}</ref> He completed a pathology research fellowship at Harvard Medical School with [[Emil Unanue]] and joined the Washington University faculty in 1985.<ref name=AAI/>

From 2005 to 2006, Allen served as the president of the [[American Association of Immunologists]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aai.org/About/History/Past-Presidents-and-Officers/PaulMAllen |accessdate=15 July 2019 |title=Paul M. Allen, PhD |publisher=AAI}}</ref> He is a member of the editorial board for ''Immunity''.

==Research==
Allen's work specializes in the study of how [[T lymphocyte]]s recognize [[antigen]]s and initiate an [[immune response]]. He and [[Emil R. Unanue]] were responsible for the discovery that [[antigen-presenting cell]]s present antigens to bind to a special group of molecules known as the [[major histocompatibility complex]].<ref name=AAI/>
